summary: St. Marks Light, Florida's Big Bend: 1842 tower, 1862-65 war raids, the Gresham keepers, and a Fish and Wildlife Service restoration open to visitors.

lens.where: replica fourth-order lens installed 12 July 2019; the original lens is on display in the refuge visitor center (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: tower completed 1842 (FWS; USLHS); the 1831 tower was replaced

access.note: Refuge open daylight with an entrance fee; keeper's quarters open Friday to Sunday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Climbing the tower is not permitted.

facts.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge)

events.note: Act of 23 May 1828 appropriates $6,000 for the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends)
First tower, built by Beal and Thayer under Winslow Lewis for $11,765; replacement accepted January 1830 (LighthouseFriends)
Station established 1831 (USLHS record)
Tower relocated inland; the current tower completed 1842 (LighthouseFriends; FWS; USLHS)
September 1843 hurricane destroys Port Leon and damages St. Marks; sturdy tower saves Keeper Hungerford's family (LighthouseFriends)
Second powerful hurricane; tower withstands it (LighthouseFriends)
Breakwater and keeper's house built (nomination; LighthouseFriends dates the dwelling replacement to 1854)
Union ships bombard the lighthouse, 15 June 1862
Union sailors burn the wooden steps in the tower (LighthouseFriends)
Union landing of 1,000 troops, 4 March 1865, a prelude to Natural Bridge (nomination); Confederates set charges in the tower (LighthouseFriends)
Tower repaired between September and December 1866 (LighthouseFriends)
New fourth-order Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends; USLHS)
Light back in operation on 7 January 1867 (LighthouseFriends)
September 1873 hurricane floods the dwelling; the Kennedy family takes refuge in the tower
Appropriation of $100,000 for works at the station; the 1922 Commissioner's report lists a rebuilt 325-foot wharf
Keeper J. Y. Gresham tows a disabled motorboat and conveys two lost men from a hunting party (Lighthouse Service Bulletin)
Coast Guard assumes responsibility for the nation's lighthouses; the Greshams stay on
Light automated (Friends of St. Marks Wildlife Refuge)
Coast Guard spends $150,000 to repair and stabilize the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends)
Transfer from Coast Guard to Fish and Wildlife Service completed 10 October 2013 (act of June 2006; LighthouseFriends)
Fresnel lens removed in November 2014 for restoration of the lantern room (LighthouseFriends)
Renovated lighthouse opens to the public 29 September 2018 (LighthouseFriends; FWS)
Replica fourth-order Fresnel lens installed 12 July 2019 (LighthouseFriends)
Relighting on 31 October 2019 (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.why: The standing tower was completed in 1842 (USLHS record: Year Tower Established 1842; Fish and Wildlife Service: current tower completed 1842). The 1831 date is the station's establishment and first tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1831 date is the station's establishment and the first tower (USLHS); the standing tower is 1842 (Fish and Wildlife Service; USLHS). The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open in the story: (1) first lighting, 1830 (LighthouseFriends, tower accepted January 1830) against 1831 (USLHS record) and 1842 (Rowlett, as a second tower); (2) reflector size, fifteen-inch (LighthouseFriends) against fourteen-inch (USLHS); (3) dwelling replacement, 1854 (LighthouseFriends) against a breakwater and keeper's house in 1853 (nomination); (4) Rowlett's directory says the tower was extended from 65 ft in 1867, which the story does not use; (5) Rowlett gives a 2016-2019 dark period; the story does not use it. The 1972 nomination is OCR'd: quotes were chosen where the OCR is clean. LighthouseFriends prints the 2016 appropriation as '$500,0000'; the story reads it as $500,000 (the sum of $550,000 less $50,000). Ann Dudley, Sarah J. Fine: the roster is the only source for the principal keeper lines; the story does not say how Ann Dudley came to the post. The 1926 Lighthouse Service Bulletin quote is from a clean page: the OCR splits the lines, so the quoted words were checked against the scan's text. The Commissioner's 1922 entry (scan p. 744) is taken from an OCR snippet of the St. Marks line; the printed page is labelled p. 44 by the corpus tool and was not visually checked. The 1895 Light-House Board cistern note is from an OCR snippet, citing the Internet Archive volume. The child's drowning is given without a name, as LighthouseFriends prints it. LighthouseFriends is a copyrighted site: facts are paraphrased; one short quotation is used (Gresham). Fact-check 2026-10-22 (sentence-by-sentence against the NRHP nomination, LighthouseFriends, the Lighthouse Service Bulletin of 1926, the USLHS record and roster, FWS, the Friends of St. Marks Wildlife Refuge, Rowlett, and the Commissioner's 1922 and Light-House Board's 1895 reports). Changed in the story: 'the third lighthouse on the spot' is now 'the third lighthouse at the station' (the 1842 tower was built farther inland, as the story says); the station's 1831 establishment date, from the USLHS record, is now stated beside the 1830 tower; the Kennedy paragraph no longer says the family kept the light through the Civil War (LighthouseFriends says David M. Kennedy returned to the post in 1867, after the war); the child's drowning follows LighthouseFriends' location ('near the yard') and does not name the child; the 2016 appropriation: LighthouseFriends prints '$500,0000' for the lighthouse itself, which the story reads as $500,000 ($550,000 less $50,000), and the 'for the tower' wording is replaced by LighthouseFriends' wording; the 1895 cistern entry is OCR ('St Maries, St, Marks Eiver'), read as the St. Marks River station, and cited at scan p. 167 (URL is the page view of the same volume); the 1922 wharf entry is cited at printed p. 44 (scan p. 744), as the corpus page index reads it. Roster: David Carey is a contractor on the USLHS roster, not a keeper, and is removed. William F. Barry and Donald D. Luedke carry the USLHS open span 'at least 1952-' and are kept as printed; they are not named in the story. Footnote numbering has no note 3, as the story has none. Living-people check: Gresham and King are named in their public role only; no other personal detail beyond LighthouseFriends' print.
